title: Engineering Drawings & BOM
summary: Orthographic projection, section views, dimensioning rules, title blocks, and bill-of-materials structure for clear manufacturing drawings.

sections.heading: The Drawing as a Contract
sections.content:
An engineering drawing is the **legal technical communication** between design and manufacturing: it fully defines geometry, size, surface finish, material, and tolerances so a part can be produced and inspected without the designer present. A good drawing is complete but not cluttered — every line answers a question, and no feature is left to interpretation.

Drawings are the input to machining (see [[machining-fundamentals|machining]]), inspection ([[metrology-and-inspection|metrology]]), and purchasing. Ambiguity here is paid for later, in scrap and rework.

sections.heading: Orthographic Projection
sections.content:
Orthographic views project the part onto mutually perpendicular planes. Almost every production drawing uses **first-angle** (ISO) or **third-angle** (ASME) projection — the projection symbol in the title block tells which. In third-angle (common in the US), the right-side view sits to the right of the front view; in first-angle it is mirrored.

Standard practice:

- Front view shows the **most characteristic shape** — the one that would be chosen to describe the part in one sentence.
- Add side and top views only if they carry **new information**. A cylindrical shaft needs one view plus a diameter symbol.
- **Hidden lines** (dashed) show internal features in views where they are not sectioned; too many hidden lines reduce clarity.
- Use **center lines** for axes, bolt circles, and symmetry.

sections.heading: Section & Detail Views
sections.content:
Sections reveal internal geometry without hidden-line clutter:

- **Full section** — cutting plane passes entirely through the part (typical for housings).
- **Half section** — one half exterior, one half cut; ideal for symmetrical parts (flanges, bosses).
- **Offset section** — the cutting plane steps to pass through multiple features (holes, slots).
- **Revolved & broken-out sections** — local reveals for ribs, webs, and small pockets.

Section rules: hatch the solid material with fine parallel lines (or ANSI/ISO patterns per material), never hatch through the cutting-plane line, and label the cutting plane (A–A) with the section name. A **detail view** enlarges a small or complex region (e.g. a thread, a groove) with a reference circle and callout.

sections.heading: Dimensioning Conventions
sections.content:
Dimensions are placed to be **readable and functional**:

- Dimension from **datum features and functional surfaces**, never from invisible or irregular edges.
- **Baseline dimensioning** (all features from one datum) holds relative position better than **chain dimensioning**, where tolerances accumulate feature-to-feature.
- Never create a **closed loop** (over-dimensioning) — one dimension must be left as the resultant or the stack conflicts with itself.
- Use feature-based dimensioning for holes (⌀ + position, see [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]]) and keep dimensions off the part outline where possible.
- Thread callouts read major diameter first: M8 × 1.25. For blind tapped holes apply the engagement rule $L_{tap} = L_{engage} + 3P$ (engagement length plus three pitches of run-out) so the tap never bottoms out.

Apply the same standards in CAD so the model, drawing, and 3D annotations stay in sync (see [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD]]).

sections.heading: Title Block & Bill of Materials
sections.content:
The **title block** is the drawing's identity card: part name and number, material, scale, sheet size, drafter and checker, date, and the **tolerance block** (general tolerances, angular tolerances, and standard referenced). Never leave the general tolerance block empty — a drawing without stated general tolerances is unbuildable.

The **Bill of Materials (BOM)** lists every component of an assembly: item number, part number, description, quantity, material, and source. Good BOM practice:

- Use an **indented (parent-child) structure** for subassemblies so a top-level BOM rolls up correctly.
- Keep **part numbers drawn, not described** — two parts with different revisions must have different numbers.
- Reference the BOM items on the assembly drawing by balloon numbers so the drawing and list are mutually traceable.

sections.heading: Revision & Change Control
sections.content:
A drawing that can change without traceability is a liability. Every drawing carries a **revision table**: revision letter, description of change, date, and approver. The change itself flows through an **Engineering Change Order (ECO/ECN)** that records what changed, why, and the disposition of affected stock (use-up, rework, scrap).

In a CAD/PDM environment, revision control also guards the **3D model and drawing pair** — only released revisions may be issued to manufacturing, and a change to the model without the drawing (or vice versa) is a configuration error. Mature shops tie the ECO to the BOM so a drawing change automatically flags every assembly that uses the part.

keyTakeaways: A drawing must fully define geometry, material, finish, and tolerances so a part is buildable without the designer present.
Use third-angle (or consistently first-angle) projection with the projection symbol shown.
Dimension from functional datums, avoid closed loops, and never omit the general tolerance block.
Maintain revision tables and ECO discipline so model, drawing, and BOM never diverge.
